en: Without dying, my eyes closed,
And my weakness became plain.
The moon waned and the days passed
As wrestling wore me down.
He terrified my people
And gave my breath no respite.
How many times he doubled my back,
How utterly he drove out my wind,
He terrified my people.
Grieving that I could not reach him,
I despaired of my borrowed life.
I let him consume all I had amassed;
Before all whose ears had heard
And whose eyes had seen,
I was called the powerless Choro.
Breaking through the herd and opening a road,
He plundered all my property.
He wrought many a violent outrage
Upon my happy, fortunate days.
He raided my horses on their pasture
And utterly laid waste my wealth.
My power exhausted, my strength gone,
I fought but could not prevail.
Writhing in shame, my wretched soul
Burned beyond endurance,
And I grew bitter with myself.
I wished to die, yet could not die,
Unable to cast away this needed life.
Those who grappled with the infidel,
The son of Sarybai, swiftly died;
A hero died when he faced him.
From the venom of the infidel
Who came out to stand guard,
All who grappled with that slave died.
I fought him alone in single combat
And was deeply aggrieved by that swine;
To be left alive where others died—
Of all that ears have heard and eyes have seen,
I have seen no such thing among mankind.
Of all that people know and nations have witnessed,
I battled with that infidel slave;
I filled myself with a lamb’s fat,
Yet found this hell unbearably vast.
I strained, but my strength was not enough;
I could not defeat that mighty one.
My death had come, yet I did not die.
Never before had I seen such hell
Upon the face of the earth.
Since my father watched and my mother bore me,
Since I became Külchoro,
Since I grew up an orphan,
And joined the ranks of men on earth,
Since I sprang up and became a hero,
The equal of heroic sons,
Since I mounted a horse with legs astride,
Became a warrior and sought the foe,
And went through life as Külchoro;
Since I girded on my keen-edged sword,
Our uncle, who stood in our father’s place,
Led me with him and made me a hero,
And made me equal to heroic sons.
By raiding, he brought me fortune;
By building, he gave me a home,
And made me a khan of noble lineage.
He delivered me from orphanhood,
And when the time came to live in joy,
Saying, “May his heart be rich with fat,”
He fed me slices of the choicest meat.
Saying, “Let no difference remain between them,”
He had me share the breast
Of my mother Kanykei equally.
She tucked a letter into her hem
And, saying, “May he grow immense,”
Gave me the name Külchoro.
She hung an amulet about my neck,
And my sorrowing mother Kanykei
Had Kanykei herself raise me.
She erased the name of slave,
Saying, “He is your brother beneath the sun,”
And restored this ruined soul.
Raising and nurturing me, she made me great,
And made me renowned throughout the world.
My weapons numbered eighty-four,
And when I struck, I struck like fire.
At the hands of me, Külchoro,
Giants died who came to wrestle,
And peoples of many nations died.
Khans died who came to grapple,
And Black Chinese and Manchus died.
Intending to wage a true battle,
The giants Chynkojo and Toltoi died.
Coming to grapple with me,
The Black Chinese host died.
From the beginning, the one God
Made me mighty throughout the world;
But in the end the Creator
Humbled me before Sarybai.
Against this infidel Sarybai,
Shooting and fighting,
No human strength sufficed,
Nor could a lion’s teeth pierce him.
When at last I took stock,
My weakness became plain;
Fighting, I could not match his might.
O mother eagle, I could not bring him down,
I could not defeat that son of a bitch.
My power left me, and I grieved;
Of this borrowed, passing life
I thus despaired.
If an unyielding enemy comes,
I shall turn my charger’s head.
Of the humiliation that came outright,
I am telling you the truth.
This is the truth of the tale begun;
This is your warrior Choro’s secret.
Lioness sister-in-law Kuyaly,
I have sung my song to you,
I have told my secret as faithfully as my creed,
I have spoken all my truth.
If you are a hero, if you are a lion,
If you are the one renowned among the people,
The leopard’s companion,
If you are my champion sister-in-law,
Then wage the battle fiercely.
From the hands of the wrathful one,
From the fatal bullet that has struck us,
From the hands of our true enemy,
From Sarybai’s venom,
From the fury of this burning hell,
From the dragon’s poison,
Spare not your life, heroic sister-in-law;
First of all, for your hero,
For the aid his strength requires,
For your child Seytek and for me,
Wage the battle fiercely.
From the hands of that venomous one,
If your strength suffices, sister-in-law,
Deliver us and save us.
The descendants of the magnanimous lion—
Do not let them vanish or be lost,
Do not lose them and end their line,
Leaving it barren as a salt waste where no grass grows.
Do not let it be said that Sarybai
Destroyed the lion hero’s line;
Wage the battle fiercely.
Fight the clash with all your might;
From death, torment, and calamity,
Preserve them yourself!
If you are a valiant one, if you are a lion,
Kuyaly of Kaiypchal,
The finest among women,
The most graceful in tasseled ornaments,
The mightiest beneath a white headscarf,
If you are that heroic sister-in-law—
Sarybai, whom you shall fight,
Trample him into the black earth.
The descendants of the dear hero—
Protect them as their mother.
Behold our condition;
Sarybai has brought disaster,
So deliver his punishment into our hands.
Wage the struggle fiercely;
From cruel oppression and calamity,
The descendants of the dear hero—
Deliver them and save them.
Take me, Külchoro, and brave Seytek
As companions at your side.
To raise the battle cry in force,
Your scattered Kyrgyz people,
Your nation’s defenders and possessions—
From the fury of painful calamity,
Deliver them and save them.
This is the secret we have told;
It is no lie, but our truth.
Sarybai has brought us suffering;
It is no lie, but our truth.
I have whetted my black tongue,
Told every secret to the end,
And poured out my song, your dear Choro.”
When Kuyaly heard this,
Her thirst for blood seized her.
“Father, my brother-in-law Külchoro,
My dwelling place is Jelpiniş,
The white tulpar is the steed I ride,
And Sarybai is the one I shall fight;
This is how the quarrel stands.
In those dark and distant days,
When your dear sister-in-law was still a maiden,
I understood what you would need.
To your heroic uncle
I became a bride pledged until Judgment Day,
And for a long time shared his life.
I knew of this deed
Of our vengeful enemy Sarybai.
That madman, the ogre’s son,
Has passed the tale down from teller to teller;
He asked for the giant beauty, daughter of Kaiypchal,
At the urging of a mischief-maker.
Winter vanished from its season;
Because of wretched me,
Those two madmen schemed
To cast the nation into turmoil
And carry me away,
Bringing conflict upon my people,
Pouring suffering upon my people,
Starting rebellion among my people,
And spreading turmoil through my land.
At the great funeral feast for my khan father,
He began the fighting at its outset,
Driving my people frantic
And many times disturbing my heart.
He ruined my funeral feast,
And left my head ringing.
He sent a matchmaker between us,
But God took that vile man.
He sent an envoy from his people,
But God took him from the earth.
They drew their bows like pouring rain
And fired arrows like hail;
When he unleashed his violent fury,
He stood and waged battle.
Destroying the people and slaughtering the nation,
They fought in bitter conflict;
There was a clamor of battle cries,
A mighty tumult of warfare.
My dear hair, long as meadow grass,
I wound and knotted atop my head,
And donned armor no bullet could pierce.
This infidel Sarybai—
I drove him headlong from Jelpiniş.
Never letting his tail touch the ground,
Never letting him walk upon the earth,
I raised a clamor that split the sky.
Unable to lodge for even two nights,
Unable to find room upon the earth,
I thrashed him like crushed grain.
I drove him out of Jelpiniş
And bound his hands without rope.
He fought in earnest, burning with rage,
Despairing of his fly-like life;
His world closed in around him,
And his valor became known.
Against this infidel Sarybai,
This is the arm that shall wrestle,
This is the foe that shall trade shots with him.”
Maiden Kuyaly said these words,
And spoke many wondrous things;
She took up her spear called Muragy,
Girded on her scabbardless sword,
And donned armor no bullet could pierce;
Her heroism became apparent.
She performed deeds of many kinds
And made ready at the word “foe.”
Wisdom came to her from the unseen,
And she set her face toward Sarybai;
This is how the matter unfolded.
